augment

/awg-MENT/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Augment means to make something greater by adding to it; to increase.

The freelance designer took on weekend tutoring to augment her income during the slow season.

Example

To draw bigger crowds, the museum plans to augment its dinosaur hall with three newly excavated skeletons.

The sentence shows augment's essential move: the hall already exists and is made greater by adding something substantial to it — no small, scheduled steps required.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

amplify: To amplify is to increase intensity or volume — you amplify a sound, a signal, or an effect. To augment is to enlarge something by adding material, numbers, or resources to it. An amplified voice is louder; an augmented staff has more people in it.

bolster: To bolster is to shore up something that is sagging or under strain — courage, a weak argument, a shaky currency. To augment is simply to make something bigger by adding to it, with no implication that it was failing. You bolster what is threatening to give way; you augment what you merely want more of.

expand: To expand is to grow larger in extent or scope, and a thing can expand all by itself — a city expands, a balloon expands. To augment is transitive and additive: someone makes a thing greater by adding something to it. Expansion is growth; augmenting is growth by deliberate addition.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

diminish: To diminish is to make smaller or lessen — the direct reverse of making greater by addition.

curtail: To curtail is to cut something back or shorten it rather than build it up.

Where it sits · how much is added — supplement → augment → magnify

supplement vs. augment: To supplement something is to add a modest extra to it, while to augment implies a more substantial enlargement.

magnify vs. augment: To magnify is to make something dramatically greater or more intense, going beyond augment's solid but measured addition.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — aug-

Root — aug-: to increase (from augere)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Augment is the purest word in this unit: its root augere means nothing other than 'to increase,' and Latin attached -mentum to form augmentum, 'an increase.' English then borrowed the whole package as a verb. That history explains this word's one oddity — unlike the nouns in this unit, augment ends in -ment yet acts as a verb, because English inherited it fully formed from Latin rather than building it with the English noun-making suffix.

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Augment is a verb despite its noun-like -ment ending — you augment a staff, an income, or a collection. Keep it distinct from its unit-mate increment: augment names the broad act of making something larger by adding to it, while an increment is one small, regular step of increase; the additions in augmenting need not be small or scheduled at all.
